# Infinity CoolMaster: full site text

Infinity CoolMaster Co., Ltd. (บริษัท อินฟินิตี คูลมาสเตอร์ จำกัด), DBD registration no. 0105566016285, registered January 2023, Bangkok, Thailand.
Office: 157/9 Soi Ari Samphan 2, Phahonyothin Road, Phaya Thai, Bangkok 10400, Thailand. Phone: +66 82 096 6595. Email: sales@infinitycoolmaster.com.
Business: Cooling-as-a-Service (chiller-as-a-service). Infinity CoolMaster designs, finances, installs, owns and operates chiller plants; clients pay for efficient cooling from the savings, with a minimum 10% energy saving guaranteed in writing and measured monthly to IPMVP. Contracts typically run 5–10 years.
First project: Platinum Pro Plastic, Nikhom Phatthana, Rayong; in testing and commissioning in November 2026.

# English

## Chiller as a service for hotels and resorts
URL: https://infinitycoolmaster.com/en/hotels/

Infinity CoolMaster, a chiller-as-a-service provider in Bangkok, installs and operates a high-efficiency chiller plant at your hotel or resort with no upfront cost. You pay for efficient cooling out of the savings, with a minimum 10% energy saving guaranteed in writing and verified every month.

### Why cooling matters so much in a hotel

In a Thai hotel or resort the chiller plant runs day and night, all year. It is usually the largest single electricity load on the property, and every baht it wastes comes straight out of gross operating profit (GOP).

Occupancy swings between check-in waves, events and quiet nights, while tropical humidity stays high. Plants are often oversized and run at fixed setpoints, so they burn energy cooling rooms and corridors nobody is using.

### How chiller-as-a-service works for hotels

- We design, finance, install and operate a high-efficiency chilled-water plant at your site. You pay nothing upfront.
- Infinity CoolMaster owns, insures and maintains the equipment for the whole contract, so it never sits on your balance sheet.
- You pay for efficient cooling out of the savings the new plant creates, so cash flow is positive from the first month.
- A minimum 10% energy saving is written into the contract and measured every month against an IPMVP-aligned baseline. If savings fall short, we pay the difference.
- Contracts typically run 5–10 years. At the end you can renew, or take ownership of the plant under agreed transfer terms.

### What we optimise on a hotel plant

- Chilled-water production matched hour by hour to occupancy, weather and the event calendar.
- Chillers, pumps and cooling towers tuned together by our Chiller Plant Management System (CPMS) and machine-learning models.
- Guest comfort first: setpoints stay inside agreed comfort limits, with alarms watched by our 24/7 monitoring center.
- Monthly savings reports your finance team and owners can audit.

Q: Do we need to invest anything?
A: No. Design, equipment, installation and operation for the life of the contract are financed by Infinity CoolMaster. You pay for cooling from the savings the system creates.

Q: Will guests notice any change in comfort?
A: Comfort limits are part of the contract. The plant is optimised inside them, and our monitoring center watches the plant around the clock.

Q: Will installation disrupt our operations?
A: No. Work is planned around your operating schedule, switchovers happen off-hours, and redundancy is kept in place throughout, so cooling never stops.

Q: What happens at the end of the contract?
A: You choose: renew the service, or take ownership of the plant under transfer terms agreed in the original contract.

Operating theatres, ICUs, laboratories and pharmacies need cooling 24 hours a day, at stable temperature and humidity. A failure is a clinical risk, not just a comfort complaint.

At the same time, an ageing chiller plant is one of a hospital’s largest utility costs, and replacing it competes with medical equipment for the capital budget.

URL: https://infinitycoolmaster.com/en/shopping-malls/

### Cooling is a mall’s largest controllable cost

Shopping malls live on comfort: shoppers stay longer in a cool, fresh building. But the cooling load swings widely with footfall, weather, cinema schedules and tenant mix, and a plant run at fixed settings wastes a large share of its energy.

Not every mall needs new chillers. Where the existing plant is in good condition, optimisation of the controls alone can deliver verified savings.

## How cooling-as-a-service pricing works
URL: https://infinitycoolmaster.com/en/pricing-model/

Cooling-as-a-Service has no upfront cost. Infinity CoolMaster funds, owns and operates the chiller plant; you pay a service fee for efficient cooling that is covered by the energy savings, with a minimum 10% saving guaranteed in writing.

### What you pay for

With Cooling-as-a-Service you do not buy chillers. Infinity CoolMaster designs, finances, installs, owns and operates the plant. You pay a service fee for efficient cooling, and the contract is structured so that the fee is paid out of the energy savings the new plant creates.

Because a minimum saving is guaranteed in writing, your total cost of cooling (electricity plus service fee) is designed to be lower than what you pay today.

### What is included

- Engineering design and the free initial audit.
- All equipment: chillers, pumps, cooling towers, controls and metering.
- Installation, commissioning and project management.
- Operation, maintenance, insurance and spare parts for the full contract.
- Our CPMS optimisation, 24/7 monitoring and monthly IPMVP-aligned savings reports.

### How the numbers are set

- Step 1 — Audit: we analyse 12 months of electricity bills and survey your plant.
- Step 2 — Baseline: we agree a baseline model with you, aligned with IPMVP, built from at least 12 months of interval data.
- Step 3 — Proposal: you receive a written offer with the guaranteed saving percentage, the fee structure and the contract terms.
- Step 4 — Every month: actual consumption is compared with the adjusted baseline. If savings fall below the guarantee, we compensate the shortfall.

### Contract terms at a glance

Your exact fee depends on your plant, load profile and tariff, so it is set in the written proposal after the free audit.

| Term | Typical arrangement |
| Upfront investment | None |
| Contract length | Typically 5–10 years, depending on plant size and scope |
| Equipment ownership | Infinity CoolMaster, for the full term |
| Maintenance and insurance | Included |
| Savings guarantee | Minimum 10%, written into the contract |
| Measurement | Monthly, against an IPMVP-aligned baseline |
| End of term | Renew, or take ownership under agreed transfer terms |

Q: Do we need to invest anything?
A: No. Design, equipment, installation and operation for the life of the contract are financed by Infinity CoolMaster. You pay for cooling from the savings the system creates.

Q: How long is the contract?
A: Typically 5–10 years, depending on plant size and scope. Longer terms let us invest in deeper upgrades and guarantee larger savings.

Q: What happens if savings fall below the guarantee?

## Cooling as a service vs buying, leasing or ESCO
URL: https://infinitycoolmaster.com/en/caas-vs-buying-chiller/

Buying a chiller means paying the full cost upfront and carrying the performance risk yourself. With Cooling-as-a-Service the provider funds, owns and runs the plant and guarantees the saving. This page compares buying, leasing, ESCO contracts and CaaS side by side.

### Four ways to get a new cooling plant

When a chiller plant reaches the end of its life, a building owner usually has four options: buy new equipment, lease it, sign an energy-performance (ESCO) contract, or move to Cooling-as-a-Service (CaaS). They differ in who pays upfront, who carries the performance risk and who runs the plant.

### Side-by-side comparison

Lease and ESCO terms vary widely between providers; the table shows typical arrangements, not any specific offer.

|  | Buy | Lease | ESCO contract | Cooling-as-a-Service |
| Upfront capital | Full cost | Low or none | Varies; often shared | None |
| Who owns the plant | You | Lessor | Usually you | Provider, for the contract term |
| On your balance sheet | Yes | Usually yes | Usually yes | No equipment asset |
| Operation and maintenance | You | You | Varies | Provider |
| Energy-performance risk | You | You | Shared, per contract | Provider, with a written minimum saving |
| Savings measurement | Optional | Rare | Usually IPMVP | Monthly, IPMVP-aligned |
| End of term | You own it | Return or buy out | You own it | Renew, or take ownership on agreed terms |

### When Cooling-as-a-Service is the better fit

- Capital is committed to your core business, not to utilities.
- You want one partner responsible for performance, operation and maintenance.
- Your finance team wants a guaranteed, measured saving rather than an engineering estimate.
- You prefer to keep plant equipment off the balance sheet.

### When buying may be better

- You have capital available and a strong in-house engineering team to operate and optimise the plant.
- You want full control of equipment choice and maintenance from day one.

Q: Is Cooling-as-a-Service the same as an ESCO contract?
A: No. In a typical ESCO contract the client often funds or owns the equipment and the ESCO guarantees savings. In Cooling-as-a-Service the provider funds, owns, operates and maintains the plant, and you pay for efficient cooling.

Q: What happens at the end of the contract?
A: You choose: renew the service, or take ownership of the plant under transfer terms agreed in the original contract.

Q: What happens if savings fall below the guarantee?
A: We compensate the shortfall. The minimum saving is written into the contract and measured each month against a baseline agreed before any work starts.

## How we measure and verify savings (IPMVP)
URL: https://infinitycoolmaster.com/en/measurement-verification/

Every saving we guarantee is measured, not estimated. We agree an IPMVP-aligned baseline with you before work starts, meter the plant continuously and report the verified saving every month; you or a third party can audit the numbers.

### Why measurement matters

A savings guarantee is only worth something if the savings can be measured in a way both sides trust. We follow the International Performance Measurement and Verification Protocol (IPMVP), the international standard for proving energy savings.

### Our M&V process

- Baseline: before any work begins, we agree a baseline model with you, built from at least 12 months of interval data.
- Adjustments: the baseline is adjusted for factors outside our control, such as weather and occupancy, as defined in the contract.
- Metering: energy and cooling output are metered continuously on the plant.
- Monthly report: actual consumption is compared with the adjusted baseline, and the verified saving is reported every month.
- Audit: the data and calculations are open to you or an independent third party.

### What happens with the result

The verified saving is compared with the minimum written into the contract. If it falls short, we compensate the difference. The same monthly data supports ESG, green-building and energy reporting.

Q: Can a third party check the savings?
A: Yes. The baseline, metering data and monthly calculations are auditable by you or by an independent third party.

Q: What happens if savings fall below the guarantee?
A: We compensate the shortfall. The minimum saving is written into the contract and measured each month against a baseline agreed before any work starts.

## Chiller and cooling glossary
URL: https://infinitycoolmaster.com/en/glossary/

Short definitions of the terms used in chiller plants, energy savings and Cooling-as-a-Service contracts. Each term has its own link, so you can share a single definition.

- **Ton of refrigeration (TR)**: A rate of cooling equal to 12,000 BTU per hour, or about 3.517 kW of heat removed. Chiller and plant sizes in Thailand are usually stated in TR.
- **kW/TR**: The electrical power a chiller or a whole chiller plant uses for each ton of cooling it delivers. Lower is better; whole-plant kW/TR includes chillers, pumps and cooling-tower fans.
- **Coefficient of performance (COP)**: Cooling delivered divided by electrical power used, both in kW. COP = 3.517 ÷ kW/TR, so a plant at 0.80 kW/TR has a COP of about 4.4. Higher is better.
- **IPLV / NPLV**: Integrated (or non-standard) part load value: a single efficiency figure that weights a chiller’s performance at 100%, 75%, 50% and 25% load. It reflects real operation better than full-load efficiency, because chillers spend most hours at part load.
- **Chiller**: A machine that produces chilled water by removing heat with a refrigeration cycle. The chilled water is pumped to air-handling units and process equipment.
- **Water-cooled chiller**: A chiller that rejects heat into condenser water, which is cooled in cooling towers. Usually the most efficient choice for large plants in hot climates.
- **Air-cooled chiller**: A chiller that rejects heat directly to outdoor air through fans and coils. It needs no cooling towers or water treatment but loses efficiency as outdoor temperature rises.
- **Cooling tower**: Equipment that cools condenser water by evaporating a small part of it into the air. It needs water treatment to prevent scale, corrosion and biological growth.
- **Chilled water**: The cold water a chiller produces and pumps around the building or process to absorb heat; it returns warmer and is cooled again.
- **Condenser water**: The water loop that carries heat from a water-cooled chiller to the cooling towers.
- **Delta-T (ΔT)**: The temperature difference between chilled water leaving and returning to the plant. A low delta-T means more water must be pumped and more chillers run for the same cooling.
- **Variable-speed drive (VSD)**: An electronic drive that changes a motor’s speed to match the load. Because pump and fan power rises steeply with speed, slowing them at part load saves a lot of energy.
- **Variable primary flow**: A chilled-water system design in which the chiller pumps vary their flow with the load, instead of running at constant flow with separate secondary pumps.
- **Magnetic-bearing chiller**: A centrifugal chiller whose compressor shaft floats on magnetic bearings, with no oil and very low friction. Typically very efficient at part load.
- **Part load**: Operation below a plant’s full design capacity. Most chiller plants spend most of the year at part load, so part-load efficiency matters most.
- **Baseline (energy baseline)**: A model of how much energy a facility would use without an improvement, built from data measured before the project and adjusted for weather, occupancy or production. Savings are measured against it.
- **IPMVP**: The International Performance Measurement and Verification Protocol: the international standard for proving energy savings by comparing actual energy use with an adjusted baseline. It offers Options A, B, C and D.
- **Measurement and verification (M&V)**: The process of metering, calculating and reporting energy savings, usually following IPMVP, so both parties can check a savings guarantee.
- **CMVP**: Certified Measurement and Verification Professional: a certification for engineers who plan and review M&V, issued under the organisation behind IPMVP.
- **ESCO**: Energy service company: a company that delivers energy-saving projects, often under an energy-performance contract that guarantees savings. The client often funds or owns the equipment.
- **Cooling-as-a-Service (CaaS)**: A model in which a provider designs, finances, installs, owns and operates a cooling plant, and the client pays for the cooling instead of buying equipment. Also called chiller-as-a-service.
- **Power usage effectiveness (PUE)**: A data center’s total energy divided by the energy used by its IT equipment. A PUE of 1.0 would mean no overhead; cooling is usually the largest part of the overhead.
- **N, N+1 and 2N**: Levels of redundancy. N is just enough capacity for the load; N+1 adds one spare unit; 2N means two complete independent systems, each able to carry the full load.
- **TOU tariff**: A time-of-use electricity tariff with a higher price in peak hours (in Thailand, generally 09:00–22:00 on weekdays) and a lower price off-peak, nights, weekends and holidays.
- **Ft charge**: Thailand’s automatic tariff adjustment for fuel and power-purchase costs, added to each unit of electricity and reviewed by the Energy Regulatory Commission every four months.
- **Designated factory or building**: Under Thailand’s Energy Conservation Promotion Act, a factory or building with an electricity meter of 1,000 kW or more, transformers of 1,175 kVA or more, or energy use of 20 million MJ a year or more. It must appoint a person responsible for energy and manage its energy use.
- **HFC refrigerants and the Kigali Amendment**: Hydrofluorocarbons are refrigerants with high global-warming potential. The Kigali Amendment to the Montreal Protocol phases them down; Thailand ratified it in April 2024.
- **Thermal energy storage**: Storing cooling as chilled water or ice, usually made off-peak at night, and using it during peak hours to cut peak electricity demand and cost.
- **Chiller plant management system (CPMS)**: Software that monitors and controls a chiller plant as one system. Infinity CoolMaster’s CPMS uses machine learning to set chillers, pumps and cooling towers for the lowest total power.

## How efficient is your chiller plant?
URL: https://infinitycoolmaster.com/en/chiller-efficiency-check/

Enter your plant’s electrical power and cooling output to calculate its kW/TR and COP and see how it compares with rough industry bands. Use readings taken at the same moment, under normal load.

### What to measure

- Electrical power (kW) of the chillers, chilled-water pumps, condenser-water pumps and cooling-tower fans, from meters or a power logger.
- Cooling output: either the TR reading from a BTU or energy meter, or chilled-water flow (m³/h) with supply and return temperatures.
- Take all readings at the same time, under normal operation, and repeat at different loads and times of day.

### How to read the result

A single reading is a snapshot. Plants spend most hours at part load, so the number that matters for cost is the average over a full year. Use this check to see roughly where your plant stands, then measure properly.

| Whole-plant kW/TR | Rough reading (water-cooled plants) |
| About 0.6–0.8 | A well-designed, well-controlled modern plant |
| About 0.8–1.0 | Reasonable, usually with room to improve |
| Above 1.0 | Typical of older or poorly controlled plants, often with large savings potential |

Q: Why include pumps and cooling towers?
A: Your electricity bill pays for the whole plant. A very efficient chiller with oversized constant-speed pumps can still make an inefficient plant, so whole-plant kW/TR is the figure that matters for cost.

Q: Are these bands a standard?
A: No. They are rough bands often quoted in engineering literature for water-cooled plants. Climate, load profile and plant type all shift them; a proper audit compares your plant with what a redesign could achieve.

Q: What if my plant scores poorly?
A: Request a free cooling audit. We analyse 12 months of bills and survey the plant; under Cooling-as-a-Service we can fund the improvement and guarantee a minimum 10% saving in writing.

## How TOU tariffs and the Ft charge affect your chiller’s electricity cost
URL: https://infinitycoolmaster.com/en/insights/thailand-tou-ft-electricity-chiller-cost/
Published: 2026-11-05

- On Thai TOU tariffs, peak hours are generally 09:00–22:00 on weekdays, exactly when chiller plants work hardest.
- Many medium and large business tariffs also charge for the highest demand in peak hours, which a chiller plant often sets.
- The Ft charge is added to every unit and reviewed every four months by the Energy Regulatory Commission.
- A more efficient plant, load-following sequencing, pre-cooling and thermal storage all cut peak cost.

Most large buildings and factories in Thailand buy electricity on a time-of-use (TOU) tariff, and every unit also carries the Ft charge. Both shape what a chiller plant really costs to run, because cooling peaks at exactly the hours when electricity is most expensive.

## How a TOU tariff works

A TOU tariff splits the day into two periods:

- Peak: generally 09:00–22:00, Monday to Friday, when the price per unit is highest.
- Off-peak: 22:00–09:00 on weekdays, plus all day on weekends and public holidays, at a much lower price.

Many medium and large business tariffs also include a demand charge based on the highest power drawn during peak hours in the month. A chiller plant that ramps up hard on a hot weekday afternoon can set that peak for the whole month.

## What the Ft charge is

Ft is Thailand’s automatic tariff adjustment for fuel and power-purchase costs. It is added to every unit of electricity, and the Energy Regulatory Commission reviews it every four months. Because it changes, the same chiller plant can cost noticeably more or less to run from one period to the next.

## Why chillers are exposed

- Cooling demand is highest in the afternoon, inside the peak window.
- Offices, malls, hotels and factories on day shifts all cool hardest on weekdays.
- An inefficient plant (high kW/TR) multiplies every peak-hour unit and pushes up the demand charge.

## What lowers the cost

- A more efficient plant: every reduction in kW/TR cuts both peak energy and peak demand.
- Sequencing chillers and pumps to the real load instead of running spare machines.
- Pre-cooling buildings before 09:00, where comfort and process allow.
- Thermal energy storage: making chilled water or ice off-peak at night and using it in the afternoon.
- Measuring energy and demand separately, so you can see which one is driving the bill.

## Savings in kWh or in baht?

Because Ft and tariffs change, a good performance contract states clearly whether savings are measured in energy (kWh) or in money. At Infinity CoolMaster the saving is measured monthly against an IPMVP-aligned baseline, and the minimum 10% guarantee is written into the contract, so tariff changes do not blur whether the plant is performing.

## Sources

- Energy Regulatory Commission of Thailand: tariff structure and Ft (presentation) (https://www.st.gov.my/contents/K2/highlights/Presentation_slides_irf/08_session%203_dr%20direk_energy%20regulatory%20commission%20of%20thailand.pdf)
- Bangkok Post: ERC review of the fuel tariff (Ft) (https://www.bangkokpost.com/business/1710643/erc-stands-pat-on-fuel-tariff-rate)

## Designated factories and buildings: what Thailand’s energy law means for your chillers
URL: https://infinitycoolmaster.com/en/insights/designated-factory-building-energy-law-thailand/
Published: 2026-11-05

- A factory or building is designated under Thailand’s Energy Conservation Promotion Act if it has meters of 1,000 kW or more, transformers of 1,175 kVA or more, or uses 20 million MJ of energy a year or more.
- Designated facilities must appoint a person responsible for energy, run an energy management system and report as required.
- The chiller plant is usually one of the largest energy users, so it is where the biggest measurable savings are.
- Confirm current requirements with DEDE, as the regulations have been amended over time.

If your factory or building is large, it may be a “designated factory” (โรงงานควบคุม) or “designated building” (อาคารควบคุม) under Thailand’s Energy Conservation Promotion Act. That status brings legal duties to manage energy, and the chiller plant is usually one of the biggest items in that work.

## Who is covered

A factory or building is designated if it meets any one of these thresholds:

- An electricity meter, or meters, with installed capacity of 1,000 kW or more.
- Installed transformers totalling 1,175 kVA or more.
- Energy use of 20 million megajoules (MJ) a year or more, from all sources.

Many mid-sized factories and most large hotels, hospitals, malls and office towers cross at least one of these.

## What is required

Designated facilities must manage their energy use under the law and its regulations. In practice this includes:

- Appointing a person responsible for energy (ผู้รับผิดชอบด้านพลังงาน); larger sites need more than one, including a senior one.
- Running an energy management system: policy, targets, measures and reviews.
- Reporting energy use and conservation results to the authorities as required.

The regulations have been amended over time, so confirm the current requirements with the Department of Alternative Energy Development and Efficiency (DEDE) or your adviser.

## Where the chiller plant fits

- In air-conditioned buildings and many factories, the chiller plant is one of the largest energy users, so it is usually where the biggest measurable savings are.
- Energy targets need measured results. A plant metered continuously, with savings verified against a baseline, gives the person responsible for energy credible numbers to report.
- Replacing an inefficient plant is often the single measure that moves the whole site’s energy figures.

## How Cooling-as-a-Service helps

That gives a designated facility both the improvement and the documented data, without capital spending, and a minimum 10% saving guaranteed in writing.

- JETRO: Royal Decree on designated factories (English translation) (https://www.jetro.go.jp/ext_images/thailand/e_activity/pdf/econdec3.pdf)
- APEC EGEEC: Thailand economy update (designated facility groups) (https://www.apec.org/-/media/Satellite/EGEEC/Files/EGEEC43_Thailand_Economy_Update.pdf)

## Cooling for food and beverage factories: process, hygiene and energy
URL: https://infinitycoolmaster.com/en/insights/food-beverage-factory-cooling/
Published: 2026-11-05

- In food and beverage plants, cooling protects product safety and quality, so reliability and stable temperatures come first.
- Chilled water serves process cooling and production-room air conditioning; cold rooms often run on separate refrigeration.
- Fixed settings, one cold loop for every load, constant-speed pumps and fouled exchangers are the usual sources of waste.
- Any change to hygiene-critical cooling should be planned, documented and verified, with redundancy kept in place.

In food and beverage production, cooling protects product safety, shelf life and quality, so reliability comes first. It is also a large and constant electricity cost, which makes efficiency worth real money.

## Where cooling is used

- Process cooling: cooling products after cooking, pasteurising or filling, and cooling process water and equipment.
- Air conditioning of processing and packing rooms, where temperature and humidity are part of hygiene control.
- Cold rooms and freezers, often on their own refrigeration systems rather than the chilled-water plant.
- Utilities: air compressors and other equipment that reject heat.

## What matters most

- Stable temperatures, because excursions can mean rejected batches.
- Hygiene: condensation and humidity control in production areas.
- Records: temperature and energy data that support food-safety audits.
- Uptime: redundancy so a single failure does not stop the line.

## Where energy is lost

- Chillers running at fixed settings regardless of production.
- One low-temperature loop serving loads that could use warmer water.
- Constant-speed pumps and fans, and fouled heat exchangers.
- Plants sized for a future expansion that never came, running at inefficient part load.

## Improving without risk

- Measure first: whole-plant kW/TR, load by shift and the temperatures each process really needs.
- Separate loads by temperature where possible.
- Add variable-speed drives and plant-wide control that follows the production schedule.
- Keep redundancy and change control: any change to a hygiene-critical system should be planned, documented and verified.

There is no capital outlay, and a minimum 10% energy saving is guaranteed in writing.

## Cooling for pharmaceutical and cleanroom production
URL: https://infinitycoolmaster.com/en/insights/pharmaceutical-cleanroom-cooling/
Published: 2026-11-05

- Cleanrooms use chilled water around the clock to hold validated temperature and humidity limits.
- High air-change rates and dehumidification make them some of the most cooling-intensive spaces.
- The biggest savings are usually in the central plant: sequencing, efficient chillers, variable-speed pumps and matching water temperature to real dehumidification needs.
- Changes to qualified HVAC follow change control, with redundancy maintained and room conditions verified.

Pharmaceutical, medical-device and electronics cleanrooms must hold tight temperature and humidity limits 24 hours a day. The chiller plant behind them is critical to compliance, and it is also one of the site’s biggest energy users.

## Why cleanrooms use so much cooling

- High air-change rates move large volumes of air through filters and coils.
- Humidity control often means cooling air well below room temperature to remove moisture, then reheating it.
- Many areas run all day, every day, whether or not production is running.

## What must never be compromised

- Temperature and humidity within the validated limits.
- Room pressure cascades and airflow patterns.
- Redundancy, so a single failure does not take a classified area out of specification.
- Change control: modifications to qualified HVAC systems follow documented assessment and requalification where required.

## Where the savings usually are

The biggest opportunities are usually in the central plant, which serves the air handlers rather than being part of the validated room conditions:

- Chiller sequencing, efficient chillers and variable-speed pumps.
- Matching chilled-water temperature to what dehumidification really needs, rather than the coldest possible water all year.
- Heat recovery from chillers for reheat, where the system allows.
- Continuous monitoring with predictive fault detection.

## Planning changes safely

- Agree the scope with quality assurance and engineering before work starts.
- Keep redundancy in place throughout any replacement.
- Document every change and the verification that room conditions stayed within limits.

## Cooling-as-a-Service vs an ESCO contract in Thailand
URL: https://infinitycoolmaster.com/en/insights/cooling-as-a-service-vs-esco-thailand/
Published: 2026-11-05

- In a typical ESCO contract the client funds or finances the project and owns the equipment, while the ESCO guarantees savings.
- In Cooling-as-a-Service the provider funds, owns, operates and maintains the plant, and the client pays for cooling from the savings.
- Both share performance risk through a guarantee; they differ in capital, ownership and who runs the plant.
- Whichever you choose, insist on a written baseline, a clear measurement method and a defined shortfall remedy.

Thai building owners who want to cut cooling costs usually meet two kinds of offer: an energy-performance contract from an ESCO (energy service company), or Cooling-as-a-Service (CaaS). Both talk about guaranteed savings, but they put the money, the equipment and the risk in different places.

## How an ESCO contract usually works

- The ESCO audits the site and proposes energy-saving measures.
- The client often funds the project, or finances it, and owns the equipment once installed.
- The ESCO guarantees a level of savings, usually measured with IPMVP, for a set period.
- Operation and maintenance may stay with the client or be contracted separately.

## How Cooling-as-a-Service works

- The provider designs, finances, installs and owns the chiller plant.
- The provider operates and maintains it for the contract term.
- The client pays for efficient cooling, with the fee designed to be covered by the savings.
- At Infinity CoolMaster, a minimum 10% saving is guaranteed in writing and measured monthly; contracts typically run 5–10 years.

## Side by side

- Upfront capital: ESCO often yours, or financed; CaaS none.
- Equipment owner: ESCO usually you; CaaS the provider during the term.
- Who runs the plant: ESCO varies; CaaS the provider.
- Performance risk: shared under both, through the guarantee.
- End of term: ESCO you already own it; CaaS renew or take ownership on agreed terms.

## Which suits you

- Choose an ESCO-style project when you have capital and a strong in-house team to run the plant, and want the asset on your books.
- Choose Cooling-as-a-Service when capital belongs in your core business, you want one partner responsible for performance and operation, and you prefer to pay for an outcome.

Either way, insist on a written baseline, a clear measurement method and a defined remedy if savings fall short. Our comparison page covers buying and leasing as well.

## Refrigerant phase-down: what it means for older chillers in Thailand
URL: https://infinitycoolmaster.com/en/insights/refrigerant-phase-down-r22-kigali-thailand/
Published: 2026-11-05

- R-22 (HCFC-22) is being phased out in Thailand under the Montreal Protocol, so recharging old R-22 chillers gets harder and costlier.
- Thailand ratified the Kigali Amendment on 3 April 2024 and committed to cut HFC production and consumption by 80% by 2045.
- Plan replacement of old R-22 chillers before a major leak forces it, and choose a refrigerant with a long future for new plants.
- Recover and dispose of old refrigerant correctly when a chiller is replaced.

Refrigerants are the working fluid inside every chiller. International agreements are steadily removing the ones that damage the ozone layer or heat the climate, and that affects how long older chillers can economically keep running.

## R-22 and other HCFCs

R-22 (HCFC-22) was the standard refrigerant in older chillers. Under the Montreal Protocol, developing countries including Thailand are phasing out HCFCs, with consumption almost entirely eliminated by 2030 and only a small servicing allowance after that. As supply shrinks, recharging an R-22 chiller after a leak becomes harder and more expensive.

## HFCs and the Kigali Amendment

HFC refrigerants such as R-134a and R-410A replaced HCFCs. They do not harm the ozone layer but have a high global-warming potential. The Kigali Amendment to the Montreal Protocol phases them down. Thailand ratified it on 3 April 2024 and committed to cut HFC production and consumption by 80% by 2045.

## What it means for a chiller owner

- An old R-22 chiller is on borrowed time: plan replacement before a major leak forces it.
- New plants should use refrigerants with a long future, such as lower-GWP HFO blends or natural refrigerants where suitable.
- Leak prevention, detection and records matter more each year.
- Refrigerant recovery and disposal must be handled correctly when a chiller is replaced.

## Choosing a refrigerant for a new plant

- Ask each supplier for the refrigerant’s GWP and its expected availability over the plant’s life.
- Compare efficiency at part load, not just full load.
- Check local service capability for the refrigerant and equipment you choose.

## Replacing without capital spending

Under Cooling-as-a-Service, Infinity CoolMaster funds and installs a new high-efficiency plant on a refrigerant chosen for the long term, recovers the old refrigerant properly, and operates the plant with a minimum 10% energy saving guaranteed in writing.

- Cooling Post: Thailand ratifies the Kigali Amendment (https://www.coolingpost.com/world-news/thailand-ratifies-kigali-amendment/)
- International Institute of Refrigeration: Thailand ratifies the Kigali Amendment (https://iifiir.org/en/news/thailand-ratifies-the-kigali-amendment)

## What is Cooling-as-a-Service (CaaS)? A plain-English guide
URL: https://infinitycoolmaster.com/en/insights/what-is-cooling-as-a-service/
Published: 2026-11-03

- Cooling-as-a-Service (CaaS) means a provider designs, finances, installs, owns and operates your chiller plant; you pay for the cooling, not the equipment.
- The service fee is designed to be covered by the energy savings, so there is no upfront investment.
- At Infinity CoolMaster contracts typically run 5–10 years, with a minimum 10% energy saving guaranteed in writing and measured monthly to IPMVP.
- At the end of the term you either renew or take ownership of the plant on terms agreed at the start.

Cooling-as-a-Service (CaaS), also called chiller-as-a-service, is a way to get a new, efficient cooling plant without buying it. A specialist provider designs, finances, installs, owns and operates the chiller plant at your building. You pay for the cooling service, usually out of the energy savings the new plant creates, under a multi-year contract.

At Infinity CoolMaster, a chiller-as-a-service provider in Bangkok, that contract typically runs 5–10 years, includes a minimum energy saving of 10% guaranteed in writing, and is measured every month against a baseline aligned with the international IPMVP protocol.

## How Cooling-as-a-Service works

A CaaS project usually follows five steps:

- Audit: the provider studies at least 12 months of electricity bills and surveys the existing plant to estimate the savings potential.
- Proposal: you receive a written offer with the guaranteed saving, the fee structure and the contract terms, and both sides agree a measurement baseline before any work starts.
- Investment and installation: the provider buys and installs the equipment, such as chillers, pumps, cooling towers, controls and meters, around your operating schedule.
- Operation: the provider runs and maintains the plant for the full term, often with software that tunes it continuously and a monitoring center that watches it around the clock.
- Verification: actual energy use is compared with the agreed baseline every month, and the saving is reported. If it falls below the guarantee, the provider pays the difference.

## What you pay for

You do not pay for equipment. You pay a service fee for efficient cooling. In a well-designed contract the fee is covered by the savings, so your total cost of cooling (electricity plus fee) is lower than before from the first month.

## Who owns the equipment?

The provider. It owns, insures and maintains the plant for the whole contract. At the end of the term you normally choose between renewing the service and taking ownership of the plant under transfer terms agreed at the start.

## How CaaS differs from buying, leasing and ESCO contracts

- Buying: you pay the full cost upfront and carry the operating and performance risk yourself.
- Leasing: the upfront cost is spread, but you still run the plant and carry the risk that it does not save what was promised.
- ESCO energy-performance contract: an energy service company guarantees savings from an upgrade, but the client often funds or owns the equipment.
- Cooling-as-a-Service: the provider funds, owns, runs and maintains the plant and guarantees the saving. Your side is the service fee.

## Who is Cooling-as-a-Service for?

CaaS suits buildings with a central chilled-water plant and a large, steady cooling load:

- Hotels and resorts, where cooling runs all year and savings flow to gross operating profit.
- Hospitals, which need 24/7 cooling and would rather spend capital on medical equipment.
- Shopping malls, where cooling is the largest controllable cost.
- Factories and cold-chain facilities, where reliability and energy-intensity targets both matter.
- Office buildings, especially when an ageing plant faces replacement.
- Data centers, where cooling efficiency drives PUE.

## What to check before you sign

- How the baseline is built, and which adjustments (weather, occupancy) are allowed.
- The guaranteed saving and exactly what happens if it is missed.
- Contract length, and your options and costs at the end of the term.
- Comfort, temperature and uptime limits the provider must respect.
- Who pays for repairs, spare parts and insurance.
- Your right to audit the data, or to appoint a third party to do it.

## The short answer

Cooling-as-a-Service turns a large capital project into a service with a guaranteed result. The provider funds and runs the plant, and you pay for efficient cooling from the savings it creates.

## What does a chiller replacement cost? The factors that set the price
URL: https://infinitycoolmaster.com/en/insights/chiller-replacement-cost-factors/
Published: 2026-11-03

- Chiller replacement cost depends far more on the building than on tonnage: redundancy, the rest of the plant, site access and keeping cooling running all add cost.
- Compare quotes on the same design load and redundancy, and on whole-plant efficiency (kW/TR) and lifetime cost, not purchase price alone.
- Check what each quote excludes: electrical upgrades, structural work and temporary cooling are common gaps.
- With Cooling-as-a-Service the provider funds the replacement and you pay for cooling from the savings.

Building owners often ask what a chiller replacement costs. The honest answer is that it depends on the building: two plants of the same tonnage can differ several times in price. This guide explains the factors that set the price, so you can compare quotes properly, and how to replace a plant without capital spending.

## 1. Capacity and redundancy

Plant size, measured in tons of refrigeration (TR), is the starting point, but the design load matters as much as the nameplate. Many older plants are oversized, so a proper load study can reduce the capacity you need to buy. Redundancy adds cost: hospitals and data centers usually need N+1 or better, which means at least one extra chiller and matching pumps.

## 2. Chiller technology and efficiency

Higher-efficiency equipment costs more to buy and less to run. Options include variable-speed drives, magnetic-bearing compressors and water-cooled or air-cooled designs. Because a chiller runs for many years, energy cost usually outweighs purchase price over its life, so compare offers on lifetime cost, not purchase price alone.

## 3. The rest of the plant

The chillers are only part of the bill. A replacement often also covers:

- Chilled-water and condenser-water pumps, often converted to variable speed.
- Cooling towers, which may be at the end of their life too.
- Pipework, valves and insulation changed to suit the new layout.
- Electrical work: switchgear, cabling and sometimes a transformer upgrade.
- Controls and metering, needed to run the plant efficiently and prove the savings.

## 4. Site conditions

Access often drives cost more than equipment does. Removing old chillers from a basement or a rooftop may need cranes, temporary openings or road closures. Structural reinforcement, noise limits and work-hour restrictions all add time and cost.

## 5. Keeping cooling running

Most buildings cannot switch cooling off. Phased installation, temporary chillers and night or weekend switchovers keep the building running but add to the project cost. Hospitals, data centers and hotels need the most careful planning.

## 6. Refrigerants and regulation

Older chillers may use refrigerants that are being phased out. Recovering and disposing of them correctly is part of the job, and choosing a refrigerant with a long future protects the new plant's value.

## 7. Operation after handover

The cheapest plant to buy is rarely the cheapest to own. Maintenance contracts, spare parts, water treatment and the skill of the operators decide whether a new plant keeps its design efficiency or slowly drifts back to the old one's performance.

## How to compare quotes

- Ask every bidder to quote against the same design load and redundancy.
- Ask for the expected whole-plant efficiency (kW/TR), not chiller efficiency alone.
- Compare lifetime cost: purchase, installation, energy and maintenance.
- Check what is excluded, such as electrical upgrades, structural work and temporary cooling.

## Replacing a chiller plant without capital spending

With Cooling-as-a-Service, Infinity CoolMaster funds, installs, owns and operates the new plant. You pay for efficient cooling out of the savings, with a minimum 10% energy saving guaranteed in writing and measured every month to IPMVP. The audit that sets the price is free: we analyse 12 months of your electricity bills and survey your plant.

## kW/TR explained: how to benchmark your chiller plant’s efficiency
URL: https://infinitycoolmaster.com/en/insights/kw-per-tr-chiller-plant-efficiency/
Published: 2026-11-03

- kW/TR is the electrical power a chiller plant uses per ton of cooling delivered; lower is better.
- Measure the whole plant (chillers, pumps and cooling-tower fans), not the chiller alone, and average it over a full year.
- As a rough guide, about 0.6–0.8 kW/TR is a well-run modern water-cooled plant and above 1.0 kW/TR usually signals large savings potential.
- COP = 3.517 ÷ kW/TR, so 0.80 kW/TR equals a COP of about 4.4.

If you want to know whether your chiller plant is efficient, one number tells you most of the story: kW/TR, the electrical power the plant uses for each ton of cooling it delivers. Lower is better.

## What kW/TR means

A ton of refrigeration (TR) is a rate of cooling equal to 12,000 BTU per hour, or about 3.517 kW of heat removed. kW/TR divides the electrical power drawn (kW) by the cooling delivered (TR) at the same moment.

- kW/TR = electrical input (kW) ÷ cooling output (TR)
- Cooling output (TR) = chilled-water flow × temperature difference, converted to tons
- COP (coefficient of performance) = 3.517 ÷ kW/TR

For example, a plant drawing 800 kW of electricity while producing 1,000 TR of cooling runs at 0.80 kW/TR, a COP of about 4.4.

## Chiller kW/TR vs whole-plant kW/TR

A chiller's nameplate efficiency covers the chiller alone. Your electricity bill pays for the whole plant:

- Chillers
- Chilled-water pumps
- Condenser-water pumps
- Cooling-tower fans

Whole-plant kW/TR is always higher than chiller kW/TR, and it is the number that matters for cost. A very efficient chiller with oversized constant-speed pumps can still make an inefficient plant.

## How to measure it properly

- Meter electrical power for every plant component, not just the chillers.
- Measure chilled-water flow and supply and return temperatures with calibrated sensors.
- Log at short intervals (for example every 15 minutes) for at least a full year, so you see part-load, seasonal and night-time behaviour.
- Calculate the weighted average over the year, not a single best moment at full load.

Plants spend most of their hours at part load, so annual average kW/TR is far more useful than a design-day figure.

## Rough benchmarks

Engineering literature often quotes approximate bands for whole-plant efficiency in water-cooled chilled-water plants. Treat them as a rough guide, not a standard:

- Around 0.6–0.8 kW/TR: a well-designed, well-controlled modern plant.
- Around 0.8–1.0 kW/TR: reasonable, usually with room to improve.
- Above 1.0 kW/TR: typical of older or poorly controlled plants, often with large savings potential.

Climate, load profile and plant type all shift these numbers, so the most useful comparison is your own plant over time, and against what a redesign could achieve.

## Where the losses usually are

- Running more chillers than the load needs, each at poor part-load efficiency.
- Constant-speed pumps and fans running at full power regardless of load.
- Chilled-water setpoints left too low all year.
- Fouled condenser tubes and poorly maintained cooling towers.
- Controls that treat each component separately instead of optimising the plant as a system.

## From kW/TR to savings

Because kW/TR links directly to electricity use, every reduction shows up on the bill. That is why it is the core metric in a savings guarantee: under IPMVP, the baseline model and monthly reports track energy use against cooling delivered, so improvements are measured, not estimated.

Infinity CoolMaster's Chiller Plant Management System (CPMS) uses machine learning to sequence chillers, pumps and towers together and drive whole-plant kW/TR down. Under our Cooling-as-a-Service contracts a minimum 10% saving is guaranteed in writing, and a free audit shows where your plant stands today.

## How long is a Cooling-as-a-Service contract, and what happens at the end?
URL: https://infinitycoolmaster.com/en/insights/cooling-as-a-service-contract-length-end-of-term/
Published: 2026-11-03

- Cooling-as-a-Service contracts at Infinity CoolMaster typically run 5–10 years, depending on plant size and scope.
- Throughout the term the provider owns, insures and maintains the plant, and the minimum saving is measured every month.
- At the end you renew the service or take ownership of the plant under transfer terms written into the original contract.
- Settle handover condition, documents, software and early-termination terms before signing.

Two of the first questions buyers ask about Cooling-as-a-Service are how long the contract lasts and what happens when it ends. Both are decided before you sign, and both affect the price.

## How long is a Cooling-as-a-Service contract?

At Infinity CoolMaster, contracts typically run 5–10 years, depending on plant size and scope. The length follows from the investment: the provider funds the equipment and recovers that investment from the service fee over the term.

- Shorter terms suit smaller scopes, such as optimising an existing plant with new controls.
- Longer terms let the provider invest in deeper upgrades, such as new chillers, pumps and towers, and usually support a larger guaranteed saving.

## What stays the same during the contract

- The provider owns, insures and maintains the plant.
- The guaranteed minimum saving (at Infinity CoolMaster, at least 10%) applies every year.
- Savings are measured every month against the agreed IPMVP-aligned baseline.
- If savings fall short of the guarantee, the provider pays the difference.

## What happens at the end of the term?

You normally have two options, both agreed in the original contract:

- Renew: continue the service, often with updated terms, equipment upgrades or a new savings target.
- Take ownership: the plant is transferred to you under transfer terms set at the start, and you operate it yourself or appoint an operator.

Because these options are written into the contract from day one, there is no surprise negotiation at the end.

## Questions to settle before you sign

- Exactly what the transfer terms are, and how the plant's condition at handover is defined.
- Which maintenance records, drawings, software and data you receive at the end.
- Whether the control software continues to work, and on what terms, after transfer.
- What happens if your building changes use, is sold or is extended during the term.
- Early-termination terms, in both directions.

## Why the end of the contract matters for the price

The provider prices the service on the expected life and value of the equipment. Clear end-of-term options let it invest with confidence, which supports a stronger guarantee. For you, they mean the plant is never stranded: you either keep a managed, guaranteed service or take over a well-maintained plant.

## Cooling-as-a-Service for CFOs: 8 questions to ask before you sign
URL: https://infinitycoolmaster.com/en/insights/cooling-as-a-service-cfo-questions/
Published: 2026-11-03

- Cooling-as-a-Service needs no upfront investment; ask the provider for the expected monthly cash flow over the whole term.
- Accounting treatment under TFRS 16 depends on the contract terms, so involve your auditor early.
- Get the guaranteed saving as a number, the measurement method (IPMVP) and the shortfall remedy in writing.
- Check who carries equipment, insurance and tariff risk, and what happens at the end of the term.

For a CFO, Cooling-as-a-Service (CaaS) is a financing and risk decision as much as an engineering one. The provider funds, owns and operates the chiller plant, and you pay for cooling out of the savings. These are the questions to ask before you sign.

## 1. What happens to our cash flow?

There is no upfront investment. The service fee is designed to be covered by the energy savings, so cooling costs should fall from the first month. Ask the provider to show the expected monthly cash flow over the full term, with and without the guaranteed saving.

## 2. How is the contract treated in our accounts?

This depends on the contract terms and must be confirmed by your auditor. Under TFRS 16 (Thailand's equivalent of IFRS 16 on leases), a contract contains a lease if it gives you the right to control the use of an identified asset. Many service contracts, where the provider owns, operates and decides how to run the plant, may not meet that test, but the answer depends on the details. Bring your auditor in early and share the draft contract.

## 3. What exactly is guaranteed?

Ask for the guaranteed saving as a number in the contract, how it is calculated and what happens if it is missed. At Infinity CoolMaster the minimum is 10%, written into the contract, and any shortfall is compensated.

## 4. How are savings measured, and can we check them?

Savings should be measured against a baseline agreed before work starts, using an international method such as IPMVP. Ask:

- How many months of data the baseline uses (at least 12 is good practice).
- Which adjustments are allowed, for example for weather or occupancy.
- Whether you or a third party can audit the data and calculations.

## 5. Who carries which risks?

- Performance risk: the provider, through the savings guarantee.
- Equipment failure, repairs and spare parts: should be the provider's.
- Insurance of the plant: should be the provider's while it owns the equipment.
- Changes to the building's use or occupancy: check how the baseline is adjusted.
- Tariff changes: understand whether the fee and the savings are measured in energy (kWh) or in money.

## 6. What happens at the end of the term?

Typically you can renew or take ownership of the plant under transfer terms set at the start. Make sure those terms, and what you receive (records, drawings, software, data), are written down.

## 7. Can the provider deliver for the whole term?

A 5–10 year contract is a long relationship. Ask about the provider's engineering team, monitoring capability, financing behind the assets and references from existing clients.

## 8. How does it support our ESG reporting?

Monthly, metered energy data and verified savings provide auditable figures for energy, emissions and green-building reporting. Ask for the report format before you sign.

## Next step
